content.title: Make higher education possible where people actually live
content.description: Sweden cannot afford to make higher education a metropolitan privilege. If we are serious about addressing skills shortages, strengthening rural areas and giving people a fair chance, policy must open the door to higher education throughout the country, not only where universities already stand.
content.extendedDescription:
Today, postcodes largely determine people's opportunities for further study. Those living near a university or higher education institution find it much easier to enter higher education than those in smaller municipalities, even though skills needs are often greatest there. This is a democratic problem and a growing obstacle to both welfare services and business.
Employers in smaller and medium-sized municipalities far from the nearest higher education institution repeatedly report difficulties recruiting teachers, nurses, engineers, social workers and other key professionals. Meanwhile, people wanting initial or further education can neither afford nor manage to move or commute to study. The gap between willingness and opportunity is widening, and politicians are responsible for narrowing it.

The question is not whether we can afford to make higher education accessible where people live. The question is whether we can afford not to.

More information: www.nyavagar.se

content.title: 3.5 years left — can insetting and auditing accelerate the transport sector's transition?
content.description: Transport must reduce emissions rapidly, and the solutions already exist. Yet they are not being chosen. Unclear accounting rules are holding back demand for fossil-free transport. Now the entire value chain is agreeing on common practice to unlock the transition.
content.extendedDescription:
Fossil-free transport is already possible through established transition solutions such as book & claim. Yet climate ambitions remain theoretical. Uncertainty about accounting, auditing and communication makes companies hesitant, and they continue buying fossil-based transport.
Transport buyers, carriers and fuel producers are now joining forces in a shared guide. It establishes clear practice for how book & claim should be accounted for and communicated so that it meets both auditors' expectations and sustainability requirements.
At the seminar, companies, industry and researchers explain the needs and obstacles. Auditors, climate experts and users examine the guide and its ability to enable real transition. Finally, the entire value chain shares what is needed to scale up and who must act next.
What has been missing is not solutions, but a shared understanding. The conditions now exist to move from ambition to impact.

content.title: AI in schools: how do we prepare pupils for working life?
content.description: AI is already part of pupils' daily lives, but four in ten teachers say their school lacks a plan for digital tools. How do we equip pupils with the digital skills working life requires, and ensure their own perspectives actually shape the response?
content.extendedDescription:
Smart tools are already a natural part of many pupils' daily lives. They use them to learn and make decisions about the future, often faster than school practices can adapt. Meanwhile, four in ten teachers say their school lacks a plan for digital tools. This creates a growing gap between pupils' reality and the education meant to prepare them for working life.

The panel focuses on what this gap means for schools' responsibility, governance and equity. How do we ensure every pupil gains the digital skills employers require? What role should pupils themselves play in shaping school practices? And how do we do this without losing quality and long-term thinking? The aim is to highlight choices needed now so that change reduces inequalities rather than deepening them.

content.title: How can properties become key players in our future energy system?
content.description: Properties could play a much greater role in the energy system. But what steps are needed to get there, what can we learn from current projects and innovations, and what benefits would success bring to society?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's combined property stock holds enormous, largely untapped potential. Through local energy production, energy storage and energy sharing, properties can become a central resource in meeting today's and tomorrow's capacity challenges. There is also potential to increase society's resilience and preparedness – something more urgent today than ever.

In an engaging on-stage discussion, we explore important energy initiatives that could pave the way for closer integration between the property sector and the energy system in the future.

content.title: Have we fished out our seas – and what is needed to reverse the trend?
content.description: Fish stocks in Skagerrak and Kattegatt have collapsed despite extensive regulation and good data availability. What does this development tell us about Sweden's fisheries management – and what political choices are needed to strengthen marine biodiversity and our future food supply?
content.extendedDescription: New research based on 75 years of fisheries data from Skagerrak and Kattegatt shows that commercial landings have fallen by more than 90 per cent since the mid-1900s. Species such as cod, herring and mackerel have declined sharply, and catches can now only be made of shellfish and certain flatfish. The seminar discusses how a lack of a holistic approach jeopardises our food supply and functioning ecosystems. What political decisions and measures are needed to reverse the trend for fish in Västerhavet?

content.title: Geopolitics in your electricity bill
content.description: Geopolitics increasingly appears in electricity bills. What happens when oil and gas markets are shaken, and how should customers and businesses in Sweden respond? What is the global situation and the extent of fossil dependence, and how do we act amid rapid change?
content.extendedDescription:
We live in a time when global conditions change rapidly, sometimes so quickly that analyses need date stamps. Energy markets respond immediately to geopolitical turmoil, and even in Sweden, with relatively low fossil dependence, households and businesses clearly feel the fluctuations.
How should we understand and respond to this? What does it mean when fossil resources increasingly become geopolitical tools in war, peace and the times in between?

We bring together perspectives from consumers, research and the energy sector. We discuss the latest geopolitical and energy market developments, Swedish electricity customers' experiences, and the role energy companies can and should play in providing security and guidance in an increasingly complex world.

content.title: More food in the north: how difficult can it be?
content.description: Northern Sweden has disused farmland, an increasingly favourable growing climate and untapped potential for food production. We need to increase food production here to make food preparedness more robust across Sweden, but how? What new knowledge and skills are needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Global instability is bringing a new focus on domestic food production. At the same time, the changing climate is opening up new opportunities for cultivation and food production in northern Sweden.

Agriculture in northern Sweden has long struggled with poor profitability and infrastructure, and has not been prioritised in national politics. Today, there is renewed interest in developing opportunities to produce more food in the north.

But agriculture in the north cannot be expanded by simply copying southern Sweden. In a recently published report on food production in northern Sweden, Jordbruksverket highlights the importance of coordinated efforts and greater knowledge. SLU has begun intensive work to develop a hub for increased food production in the north: production that is sustainable, resilient and profitable. How can this be ensured? What knowledge is needed?

content.title: From niche players to a space cluster — can Sweden become a leading space nation?
content.description: Space is not just an important industry of the future; it is part of Europe's infrastructure, economy, security and climate transition. content.extendedDescription: Over many years, Sweden has built a strong ecosystem of expertise in space and satellite systems, from launch capabilities and satellite platforms to ground infrastructure. content.title: Electrifying long-distance transport — more than a transition issue
content.description: The electrification of transport needs to accelerate — for the climate, resilience and Sweden's competitiveness. Climate policy, preparedness and industrial policy must be aligned. How do we achieve this?
content.extendedDescription:
Long-distance road transport is now ready to be electrified. The seminar presents findings from the E-Charge project showing how food deliveries can now run on electricity from Helsingborg - Stockholm and how vehicles can use high-power charging (MCS) during the driver's statutory break. The technology is here and we are ready to make the transition, for the climate, industry and perhaps also our preparedness. But long-term ground rules are needed to reduce uncertainty for those investing in vehicles and chargers.

The seminar includes representatives of the vehicle industry, transport buyers, charging operators, haulage companies and politics.
Proposals for policy instruments will be presented and discussed. It is an election year, after all!

content.title: Without the Internet of Things, Sweden stops
content.description: Sweden already depends on connected data flows. Healthcare is digitalising, cities are becoming smarter and digital technology, including artificial intelligence, increasingly shapes national security and preparedness. None of this works without robust Internet of Things infrastructure.
content.extendedDescription:
The Internet of Things, or sensor-based infrastructure, has become a quiet prerequisite for welfare, security and competitiveness. Sweden depends on it functioning. Yet connected systems and services are still treated as separate IT projects rather than critical societal infrastructure.

The public sector is expected to take extensive responsibility for essential functions, data management and continuity amid rapid technological change. The panel addresses three questions:

• What does it mean to view IoT as critical societal infrastructure?
• Why has this become a neglected issue, despite IoT infrastructure being crucial to Sweden's resilience, digital transition and growth?
• How can the public sector take responsibility when technology advances faster than regulation and procurement?

The seminar brings together the public sector, academia and business.

Coffee and sandwiches will be served from 09:30.

content.title: Swedish industry in an uncertain world – geopolitics, trade and the path to stronger competitiveness
content.description: Swedish industry has long been hit hard by the challenging geopolitical and trade policy situation. The situation is currently even more difficult because of unrest in the Middle East. These developments have resulted in weak demand and more redundancy notices.
content.extendedDescription:
Global competition has also intensified, particularly from China, where state support is contributing to downward price pressure in the European market.

German industry, which is central to Swedish exports, is also affected by weak demand, changing trade patterns and increased competition, with direct consequences for Swedish industry.

Meanwhile, new EU trade agreements have the potential to strengthen export opportunities over time, although their effects remain uncertain.

The seminar provides an up-to-date overview and discusses dependence on Germany, China's global influence, and whether these developments are temporary or structural. The focus is on strategic choices to strengthen competitiveness.

content.title: When freedom is threatened, democracy is threatened
content.description: The threat to democracy. Artistic, academic and editorial freedom are crucial to democracy.
content.extendedDescription:
Dramaten and Stockholms universitet jointly highlight the crucial role of academic, artistic and editorial freedom in democracy.
Internationally, we see free art and independent research being restricted, with serious consequences for democratic society. In Sweden too, the arm's-length principle is challenged. Universities and cultural institutions face increased political control, researchers warn of threats to independent research, and culture is squeezed by historically low funding and new financing models.
Meanwhile, public debate is weakened by polarisation, disinformation and online hate. Journalists, researchers and artists are threatened into silence, and silence itself is a threat to democracy.

content.title: Northern Sweden's basic industries deliver – if policymakers act
content.description: Industry's operating conditions are crucial to Swedish growth. Investment continues in the north, and industry's skills needs are growing. Yet the international outlook is uncertain. Success requires the right framework conditions. What reforms should a new government implement after the election?
content.extendedDescription:
Ahead of the parliamentary election on 13 September, the focus must be on growth, which is crucial to Sweden's long-term prosperity. Industry is the economy's backbone: investment drives innovation, strengthens production and increases demand for skills. Industry needs the right skills, more hours worked and stable rules. Meanwhile, political proposals risk raising costs and inhibiting productivity in an uncertain global environment of geopolitical turmoil and increased competition. Productivity growth is already weak, particularly in basic industries.

What reforms strengthen competitiveness, reduce matching problems and increase mobility towards industrial jobs in the north? What incentives encourage people to move where the jobs are? What reforms can actually increase labour supply? Industry also depends on international skills. Yet a salary floor for labour migration is being introduced – are policymakers prepared to pursue measures that risk making skills provision harder?

content.title: People-centred climate adaptation: how can we protect vulnerable groups?
content.description: A changing climate brings more extreme weather and greater risks to lives, health and homes. Reducing vulnerability requires lower emissions and preventive work to strengthen preparedness. Climate adaptation is about preventing risks and protecting people, especially those hardest hit by crises.
content.extendedDescription:
Extreme weather causes more than material damage. It also affects people's health, sense of security and ability to manage everyday life, for example during heatwaves, floods and prolonged societal disruption. When society's protection falls short, already vulnerable groups are often hit hardest.

A new report from Röda Korset highlights the unequal impacts of climate change and the need to strengthen preparedness. As the Nordic region's largest insurer, If sees daily how extreme weather affects people and property. Meanwhile, important Nordic experience shows that prevention and climate adaptation can reduce risks.

During Almedalen, Röda Korset and If bring together public authorities, business and civil society to discuss how to strengthen society's resilience and better protect the most vulnerable.

content.title: Culture and creativity as a transformative force in societal transition
content.description: Northern Sweden is undergoing a major societal transition. How can culture strengthen participation, attractiveness and resilience, and how can we harness the cultural and creative industries' driving forces in this transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Societal transition in northern Sweden involves major investments, but also a growing need for inclusion and participation to create sustainable living environments. Culture plays a central role in democracy, attractiveness and resilience. The seminar starts from culture's role in societal transition, drawing on experience from northern Sweden. Cultural and creative industries contribute crucial skills. The question is whether innovation systems are equipped to harness them. Addressing complex societal challenges requires better-targeted innovation support based on these industries' exploratory, cross-sectoral and boundary-crossing ways of working.

How does culture contribute to resilience and attractive communities? How must the innovation system adapt to fully harness the driving forces of cultural and creative industries?

Drawing on northern Sweden, we highlight paths towards a more inclusive innovation system regionally, nationally and in cooperation with Europe.

content.title: Economic developments and monetary policy – what are the consequences for municipalities and regions?
content.description: Municipalities and regions with large loans can be affected by rising interest costs. We want to highlight this, explain the current situation and explore what today's economic conditions mean for Riksbanken's monetary policy considerations.
content.extendedDescription:
In a turbulent world, interest rates may need to rise quickly, potentially causing sharply higher interest costs for municipalities and regions with large loans and short fixed-rate periods. What is the situation now, and what do current economic conditions mean for Riksbanken's monetary policy considerations? How often should we expect Riksbanken to change interest rates going forward?

In this seminar, we hear from Deputy Governor Aino Bunge, who provides an up-to-date picture of the economic situation and its implications for lending to households, businesses, municipalities and regions.

Immediately after the address, we offer light refreshments, drinks and opportunities to network until 18.45.

content.title: How do we ensure sound financial management in municipalities and regions?
content.description: Sweden has around 40 000 elected local politicians, about 90 per cent serving alongside work or studies. Elected representatives bear ultimate responsibility for municipal and regional finances, but are they offered sufficient training?
content.extendedDescription:
Are you an elected representative? Join a Q&A and demonstration of Kommuninvest's training platform KI-akademin for municipalities and regions. Sweden has around 40 000 elected representatives, about 90 per cent serving alongside work or studies. The sector's debt is around SEK 959 billion, giving it substantial financial responsibility. Ultimate responsibility rests with elected representatives on executive boards, committees or council preparatory bodies. Kommuninvest promotes sound financial stewardship by strengthening the sector's financial management. It offers free training to improve decision-making and dialogue between elected representatives and officials.

content.title: Young people vote with their feet: from leisure to the future
content.description: Young people vote with their feet every day, but are we really listening? When some never join leisure activities or leave early, it affects their path into education and work. Why is this? How do we build systems that bring more people into communities where they develop skills for working life?
content.extendedDescription:
Young people vote with their feet every day, but are we really listening?

When children and young people choose activities, return to some settings or leave others, they tell us something important about their needs, interests and dreams. But do we use this knowledge when developing tomorrow's leisure activities?

Meanwhile, many young people remain outside leisure activities or leave them early. The consequences emerge later as reduced participation, weaker networks and fewer opportunities to develop skills that matter in education, work and society.

The seminar brings together young people, municipalities, civil society and business to discuss how we build stronger bridges between leisure and the future. How can we listen better to young people? What role does leisure play in democracy, community and hope for the future? And how can we help more young people develop, make their voices heard and find their way forward in life?

No preparation is required.

content.title: How can different societal stakeholders work together on voluntary return migration?
content.description: Returning to your country of origin when you hold a Swedish residence permit is a major decision for many people, and a fundamental right. Support is available for those who want it, but getting there requires knowledge, trust and collaboration.
content.extendedDescription:
Migrationsverket and the national coordinator for voluntary return migration invite you to a discussion on how different stakeholders – authorities, municipalities and civil society – can work together to create the right conditions for individuals to make well-informed decisions. Some time has passed since efforts intensified. What have we learned? What do the statistics show about the return migration grant increased on 1 January, and how do applicants experience the process? content.title: Digital trust and federated infrastructure — the key to secure cooperation between organisations
content.description: The public sector and businesses increasingly need to share data and use common services. How does digital trust make this easier? How do we create infrastructure that enables secure cooperation without every organisation building its own solutions?
content.extendedDescription: The ability to share data between government agencies, municipalities, regions and businesses is essential to greater efficiency and societal security. Many different solutions are used today, leading to inefficiency and increased costs. Federated solutions are presented as the route to digital trust in complex ecosystems, but trust requires shared ground rules, clear governance and enough connected organisations. A federation creates value only when many members and service providers participate. In this seminar, we discuss how national federated infrastructure can enable secure and efficient cooperation. The discussion draws on experience from Digg's work with Ena and Samordnad identitet och behörighet, as well as findings from a recent PwC report. The focus is on benefits to society across sectors in a more connected digital Sweden.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Skills supply determines Sweden's life sciences position — what is needed now?
content.description: Sweden wants to lead in life sciences, but skills shortages hold back innovation, healthcare development and competitiveness. The strategy points the way but is not enough. Reaching the goals requires political priorities, cooperation and clear responsibility for skills supply.
content.extendedDescription: Securing skills in Swedish life sciences requires political priorities and cooperation between academia, healthcare and business. Needs range from medical and biomedical expertise to AI, data and digital health, as well as healthcare staff who can drive research and innovation — something today's systems do not fully meet. Life sciences and healthcare depend on one another: without the right skills, development stalls; without innovation, quality risks declining. Meeting these needs requires better analysis, future-oriented education, clear career paths, lifelong learning, stronger clinical research and the ability to attract international talent. What political choices are needed, how can cooperation be strengthened and responsibilities clarified? The seminar brings together stakeholders seeking to contribute solutions and strengthen Swedish competitiveness and patient benefit.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for Sweden's largest workplace?
content.description: At 600,000 kilometres, the road network is by far Sweden's largest workplace. But how do we stop human exploitation and safeguard drivers' working conditions when visibility into their working environment is minimal?
content.extendedDescription:
Hundreds of thousands of drivers use the road as their daily workplace, often under conditions that are difficult for authorities to monitor. There are clear indications that drivers are forced to work extremely long shifts and live in inadequate conditions, but the lack of oversight means we know too little about what actually happens behind the wheel.

As roadside checks decline, an uneven market emerges in which unscrupulous operators can exploit drivers' vulnerability without risking penalties. This threatens not only individual drivers but the entire legitimate transport industry.

The seminar discusses how we can increase oversight and strengthen drivers' conditions. What is required of policymakers and authorities to ensure laws and regulations are actually followed throughout Sweden's road network?
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: When others cut back – why do some municipalities and regions invest in culture?
content.description: When cultural budgets are questioned and culture's share of the state budget is at its lowest in over 25 years, some choose to move in the opposite direction. Why?
content.extendedDescription:
According to trade union DIK's cultural report, Umeå, Malmö and Västra Götalandsregionen invest the most in culture. Why do some municipalities and regions prioritise culture while the state reduces its investment? Is culture a luxury in difficult times, or an investment in democracy, public health and social cohesion?
This conversation brings together politicians from three of Sweden's highest-investing municipalities and regions in culture to discuss what actually happens to a community when culture is strengthened, and what is at stake when it is deprioritised.

content.title: Veterinary care at any price: who is responsible, and can pet owners afford to wait?
content.description: Sweden has one of the EU's highest rates of veterinary price increases. Emergency care prices have risen by up to 50% in five years, putting considerable pressure on pet owners.
content.extendedDescription:
When the cost of saving an animal's life jeopardises household finances, both animal welfare and trust in the system are at stake. In February, Konkurrensverket found inadequate price transparency and weaker consumer protection for pet owners than for almost any other service. The government responded by instructing Konsumentverket to improve price information. In a market characterised by price rises and limited transparency, an urgent question arises: must industry actors take responsibility and regulate themselves, or is political intervention needed? What role do insurers and pet owners play in the cost spiral affecting more and more households?

Industry representatives, decision-makers, insurers and representatives of the dog community discuss how greater transparency and new forms of cooperation can become reality. By bringing together those with the power to make changes, we focus on decisions rather than analysis. One thing is certain: pet owners will soon be unable to afford to wait.

content.title: Effective scrutiny of non-profit associations through bank data
content.description: Welfare fraud and hidden networks threaten the voluntary sector. When unscrupulous actors exploit the system and information-sharing falls short, old routines are not enough.
content.extendedDescription:
Non-profit associations play a crucial role in Swedish society, but this organisational form can also be misused for tax and benefit fraud and as a cover for hidden networks. Traditional checks are not always sufficient to distinguish legitimate organisations from risky ones before harm is done.

- What is needed to build trust without being naive?

content.title: Longer lives, shorter working days – an impossible pension equation?
content.description: Sweden needs more people to work longer, yet many doubt they can keep going until retirement. Young people struggle to enter the labour market, while older people who want to work struggle to find jobs. Many also want shorter working days, but knowledge of how life choices affect pensions is limited. How can the equation add up?
content.extendedDescription:
Drawing on Globeknot's first report, we discuss how Sweden can meet simultaneous challenges: longer lives, later entry into employment, AI-driven transformation and a growing need for flexibility and career change.

The starting point is creating sustainable, inclusive working lives throughout life, enabling more people to work longer and giving them knowledge to make informed choices about work, working hours and retirement. How can flexibility be combined with financial security without eroding pension levels? The seminar focuses on links between working conditions, preventive health, life choices and pensions, and the changes needed for working life to function for young people, those mid-career and older people in a changing society.

content.description: Civil aviation is transitioning to sustainable aviation fuels, SAF. How does this affect Sweden's and NATO's preparedness and security of supply?
content.extendedDescription:
Civil aviation is transitioning to sustainable aviation fuels, SAF. How does this affect Sweden's preparedness and Försvarsmakten's needs? The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz clearly demonstrates how global fossil fuel supply chains can quickly be disrupted. How and when could Sweden become self-sufficient in aviation fuels? What is NATO's view?

The EU has adopted ReFuelEU aviation to reduce aviation's climate impact by gradually increasing the share of sustainable aviation fuels. By 2050, 70 per cent of all aviation fuel in the EU must be sustainable (SAF), including 35 per cent eSAF (electricity-based). Sweden has unique conditions that could make it a world-leading producer of eSAF.

Currently, aircraft are only approved to use blends containing up to 50 per cent SAF, but the industry has stated its intention to reach 100% by 2030. As early as 2017, the JAS 39 Gripen made a test flight on 100 per cent SAF. How does the Swedish defence industry view these opportunities?

content.title: How do we secure skills and capacity in Sweden's defence sector?
content.description: Growing geopolitical tensions and major defence investments are creating a new situation. Defence organisations need to rapidly expand their efforts to attract, develop and retain the right skills. What is needed to secure skills supply in a new security reality?

content.title: When AI determines the future, how does Sweden take the lead?
content.description: Skills, infrastructure and green energy give Sweden a strong starting point in AI. A well-balanced regulatory framework for the AI market can become a competitive advantage, but requires wider adoption and greater investment. What is needed for Sweden to move from cautious user to leading AI nation?
content.extendedDescription:
AI, data, critical digital infrastructure and cybersecurity have become strategic resources, not only for innovation and growth but also for national security, sovereignty and resilience.

Sweden has strong digital foundations and a national AI strategy aiming to become one of the world's top 10 AI countries and the world leader in using AI in public administration. Yet EY's global AI Sentiment Index 2026 shows Sweden lagging behind: only 37 per cent of Swedes feel comfortable with AI, compared with 49 per cent globally, only 15% use AI daily at work and 6 in 10 lack AI training.
The gap is therefore less about technology and more about trust, skills and practical application in business, politics, the public sector and academia.

During the seminar, we discuss how Sweden can strengthen its competitiveness and international position through responsible governance, broad skills development and safe, accelerated AI adoption.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: What is needed for regions to succeed in building world-leading life science clusters?
content.description: Sweden wants to lead in life sciences, but is losing ground in introducing new medicines. Rapidly bringing innovation into healthcare determines our international strength. Can research clusters flourish without leading clinical development?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's metropolitan regions want to build world-leading life science clusters. Success requires a willingness to lead development, not merely follow it. The introduction of new medicines is slowing faster in Sweden than in comparable countries. Reversing the trend requires better conditions for rapidly implementing new therapies.

An innovation cluster is only as strong as its ability to turn innovation into clinical benefit and attractiveness. Some regions want to lead, but national support is not always sufficient. Sweden could establish a unique ecosystem of testbeds. Earlier introduction of medicines gives patients faster access to breakthroughs while making clinical trials more attractive.

Is it a strength that some regions lead the way, or are better national conditions needed throughout the country? How can we secure international competitiveness?

The seminar is a collaboration between BMS, Roche and Takeda.

content.title: The competition for talent
content.description: Access to the right skills is crucial to growth and innovation. How do we make the Öresund region more attractive and inclusive? Sweden and Denmark need to act together to create a dynamic, inclusive labour market that attracts global talent.
content.extendedDescription:
Skills supply is one of the most important future issues for Swedish and Danish competitiveness. The Greater Copenhagen labour market region offers unique opportunities, but also clear barriers, to attracting and retaining the right skills. In a time of global competition for talent, Sweden and Denmark need to act together, not in parallel.
How can we strengthen cooperation between Sweden and Denmark to meet business needs? How can national actors, regional initiatives, municipalities and businesses cooperate more effectively?

The panel's questions align with the ongoing Cross-border Talent Bridge initiative, led by Lunds kommun in cooperation with Köpenhamns kommun, Medicon Village Innovation, Ideon Science Park, OpenTech and Medicon Valley Alliance, and co-financed by the Interreg Öresund–Kattegat–Skagerrak programme.

content.title: From potential to practice: when new technologies such as AI become critical to society
content.description: What requirements must be set for infrastructure, data centres, storage, secure networks, connectivity, data and governance so that new technologies such as AI can be deployed in essential services?
content.extendedDescription:
As society becomes deeply digitalised, at a time of rapid technological development, growing cyber threats and increased demands for resilience, it is no longer enough for each individual component to work on its own. It becomes crucial for the entire digital chain to hold together. Healthcare, energy, finance and other essential services now depend on interconnected infrastructure in which data centres, storage, communications layers such as 5G and secure networks, operations, procurement and next-generation technologies such as AI must work seamlessly together and withstand pressure.

This discussion brings together decision-makers from the public sector, business and politics to consider whether Sweden's digital capability will hold up as new technologies move into the most critical services, and what is needed for every layer of the chain to perform. How do we combine rapid innovation with control, security and long-term societal resilience?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: What is the government doing to save snus in the EU?
content.description: Several EU countries are moving towards banning or restricting snus. The government says it is fighting for snus, which is manufactured in Sweden and used by many Swedes. The opposition, by contrast, believes the government has not done enough.
content.extendedDescription:
Snus has become a hot political issue. France has introduced a total ban making snus use punishable by substantial fines. Other countries are preparing similar rules against snus. At EU level, proposals also include major restrictions and tax increases.
For Swedes who use snus, this can create major problems when travelling, while also reducing export opportunities and jobs in Sweden.
The Swedish government says it is fighting for snus in the EU. The opposition says the government has not done nearly enough. To find out what Sweden is doing – or should do – to save snus, we are organising an open political debate on the subject!

content.title: Knowledge without borders – with geopolitical border guards
content.description: Research cooperation with so-called difficult countries places academia in a field of tension where ethics, security, research quality and global knowledge development collide. What opportunities and risks does research cooperation involve, and how can academia act when research and geopolitics become intertwined?
content.extendedDescription:
Research cooperation with so-called difficult countries places academia in a complex field of tension where ethics, security, research quality and global knowledge development collide. International partnerships can provide access to new technology, data, infrastructure and expertise – but also entail risks such as political influence, misuse of technology and unwanted dependencies.
Yet refraining from cooperation is not without problems either. It can protect academic integrity, but risks isolating research communities, weakening dialogue and making shared solutions to global challenges harder to achieve.
In this seminar, we explore both opportunities and pitfalls and discuss how academia can navigate a world in which research and geopolitics are becoming increasingly intertwined.
• How should academia act when research and geopolitics become interwoven?
• Who is best placed to make the difficult judgements about international research cooperation?

content.title: Tall timber buildings showing that sustainable architecture is possible in a dense inner-city setting
content.description: Tall timber apartment buildings offer good opportunities to develop more sustainable construction, but also present challenges associated with the conditions of a dense, high-rise inner-city environment. What are the most important issues, and what lessons can we take into the timber architecture of the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Cederhusen is a residential project completed in 2024 in Hagastaden, Stockholm. It comprises 245 apartments across two blocks with four buildings, the tallest reaching 13 storeys. With 8,798 cubic metres of Swedish-produced cross-laminated timber, it is one of the world's largest urban solid-timber projects. The project was designed by General Architecture for housing developer Folkhem.
The site was considered technically complex, making lightweight timber construction a suitable solution. The project took a long time and involved major challenges, both structural and financial. Key issues included durability, structure, fire, acoustics, wind, moisture, light, safety and climate throughout every stage.
The result is buildings that clearly demonstrate the possibilities of timber and create a living environment rooted in Stockholm, architectural history and the new district. The experience has provided valuable insights into the potential and challenges of timber architecture. The talk is given by an architect responsible for the project at General Architecture.

content.title: From possibility to reality – how can new ways of working meet growing care needs?
content.description: Swedish healthcare is at a crossroads. An ageing population, increasing use of medicines and a shortage of healthcare staff are putting pressure on a system already working flat out. Meanwhile, technologies and solutions exist that enable earlier, more preventive and safer care at home.
content.extendedDescription:
Smart sensors and automated medication management can ease the workload of health and social care staff while helping more people manage their own care. The next generation of home-based welfare technology is already on the doorstep. It will also improve care quality through better remote care, increased prevention and continuous monitoring of health status.
But new innovations are being introduced slowly. Regulations and reimbursement models are poorly adapted to new technology, and health and social care services struggle to adopt new ways of working. The central question that must be answered is: how do we turn the potential of new technology in health and social care into reality?
Join an honest, unfiltered discussion of welfare technology as we bring the conversation often held behind the scenes in Almedalen onto a stage in Folkhälsodalen.

content.title: When simplicity meets security – balancing business freedom and crime prevention
content.description: The balance between making entrepreneurship easy and combating financial crime.
content.extendedDescription:
Many politicians talk about making it easier to start and run businesses. But have we missed the point? Perhaps it is more about making life harder for criminals and more profitable for those following the rules. The seminar explores the balance between making entrepreneurship easy and combating financial crime.

What tensions arise when combining simplicity for entrepreneurs with protection against fraud and financial crime? Can digitalisation create systems that make doing the right thing natural and wrongdoing difficult, and how can we prevent complex legacy systems from being easy to manipulate?

How far can and should we go in pursuing criminals without stifling entrepreneurship? And how can smart digital solutions increase security while simplifying everyday life for business owners?

content.title: Tech giants under pressure?
content.description: More countries are introducing or considering age limits for social media to protect children and young people. Meanwhile, tech companies such as Meta have been found liable in court and fined billions for inadequate protection and known risks of sexual exploitation.
content.extendedDescription:
Tech giants face increasing political and legal pressure over their responsibility for children's and young people's safety online. International court rulings and regulatory initiatives reveal a growing conflict between platforms' business models and society's demands for protection.
Algorithms now control content distributed to children and young people, helping shape norms concerning women, girls, misogyny, appearance and sexuality. This includes exposure to pornographic material that normalises violence and degradation, and environments where sexualised violence can spread and intensify.
In supporting women and girls, Unizon's member support centres have long encountered the consequences of a digital environment that shapes, reinforces, spreads and normalises severe sexual violence, while responsibility for addressing these problems has largely been placed on young people themselves.
How are children and young people affected? What responsibilities do tech companies have, and which do they take? What demands can and should society make going forward?

content.title: Are we staying on course? Climate targets, urban development and the economy's new playing field
content.description: Sweden has ambitious climate targets, but the pace of the transition is being questioned. As geopolitics, energy needs and economic uncertainty put pressure on decision-makers, how do we stay on course towards net zero?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has ambitious climate targets, but the pace of the transition is being questioned. As geopolitics, energy needs and economic uncertainty put pressure on decision-makers, how do we stay on course towards net zero?
Meanwhile, the built environment – our cities, properties and infrastructure – accounts for a significant share of emissions. Architecture therefore plays a crucial role in the transition, from material choices and design to planning compact, resilient and energy-efficient communities. How can architecture and urban development help reduce climate impact, strengthen quality of life and drive innovation?
What role do the energy system, capital, innovations and civil society play? And how do we ensure the green transition is both competitive and fair, particularly in designing the built environments of the future?
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Sudan – the world's largest humanitarian catastrophe?
content.description: How can cooperation between governments, the UN, civil society and business strengthen the response in Sudan, where one of the world's largest humanitarian catastrophes has left over 30 million people needing support, more than half of them children whose homes, schools and families have been torn apart by conflict?
content.extendedDescription:
The crisis in Sudan is marked by massive internal displacement, lack of protection and collapsed public services. Despite this, the crisis is severely underfunded and receives limited international attention.

Sweden is an important humanitarian donor, channelling support through the UN and civil society organisations, including UNHCR and Rädda Barnen.

This conversation brings together some of the stakeholders with experience of navigating the Sudan crisis.

content.title: Gaza — from emergency relief to reconstruction
content.description: One of the world's most acute humanitarian crises is unfolding in Gaza.
content.extendedDescription:
A recent UN report shows that more than 370 000 homes have been destroyed or damaged, 60 per cent of the population has lost their homes and 1.9 million people are displaced. Children make up roughly half of those forced to flee their homes and seek shelter. While people in Gaza live in humanitarian distress, the country's economy has shrunk by 84 per cent, and reconstruction is estimated to require USD 71 billion.

Sweden is a significant humanitarian donor and has recently increased its support to UN agencies, including UNDP. Among other things, this has enabled the delivery of around 4 000 temporary homes (RHUs), demonstrating how Swedish aid can translate into tangible effects on the ground.

But many challenges remain, and several humanitarian organisations struggle to operate in Gaza because of major restrictions imposed by the authorities and military.

How can Swedish organisations and Swedish aid meet the urgent shelter needs of children and families while laying the foundations for recovery in today's Gaza?

content.title: Sweden's future in the Arctic: the need for a new research icebreaker
content.description: Sweden's only research icebreaker, Oden, is approaching the end of its technical service life. The situation is critical and a political decision is urgent. Without a successor, Sweden risks losing its internationally leading position in polar research and its influence in the Arctic.
content.extendedDescription: Sweden is a leading polar research nation, contributing to international climate and environmental research addressing major societal challenges. Through this, we have built a unique capacity to operate in the Arctic Ocean. As the Arctic security situation deteriorates, this capability has gained geopolitical importance. A Swedish polar research icebreaker is key to maintaining a presence and strengthening Sweden's and its allies' combined capacity. Procuring a new Swedish research icebreaker is necessary to maintain and develop these capabilities. It is also important for infrastructure projects relevant to Europe's digital sovereignty. Procurement is complex and time-consuming, while demand is increasing and costs risk rising. Decisions therefore need to be made soon. The seminar discusses the way forward, the risks of delay and how Sweden can secure long-term, cost-effective access to a new icebreaker.
content.subject: Research

content.title: Are we governing welfare effectively? The interplay between municipalities, regions and central government
content.description: Swedish welfare is governed at several levels. This has built our local democracy. At the same time, multilevel governance requires close interaction between central government, regions and municipalities. How can our governance model ensure both effective and equitable welfare in small and large municipalities and regions nationwide?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's multilevel governance, involving municipalities, regions and central government, has been important in building today's welfare system and underpins local democracy. But governing welfare at several levels also requires close interaction between central government, municipalities and regions, whose needs can vary greatly across the country. There is a significant risk of inefficiency when central government dictates in detail how a municipality must perform a task.

Which issues are best resolved nationally and which locally to ensure equitable welfare nationwide?
How do we create a governance model that works for both small and large municipalities and delivers the best and most equitable welfare for every tax krona? And what is required of municipalities, regions, government and public agencies to make it work in everyday practice?

content.title: How waiting lists in Swedish eye care can be shortened
content.description: Swedish eye care is under severe pressure. Needs are growing faster than capacity due to an ageing population, long waiting times and major regional differences. Today, one in three patients does not receive specialist care within the healthcare guarantee.
content.extendedDescription:
These developments risk deepening inequality and worsening eye health across large parts of the country.

The seminar discusses organising eye care more efficiently to meet future needs. Could a national strategy, more efficient care processes and greater cooperation with private optometrists shorten waiting lists? What lessons can be learned from dentistry's development? The conversation focuses on how earlier detection, structured follow-up and better use of optometrists' expertise can relieve specialist services, improve access and secure more equitable eye care throughout the country.

content.title: Different childhoods, different futures — what is needed to give every child a good start?
content.description: Most children in Sweden are doing well, but not all. Children whose needs are not identified in time often face several challenges. When support from society fails to arrive, the risks of poorer health, weaker school results and diminished confidence in the future increase. What do our youngest children need, and what must we change to provide it?
content.extendedDescription:
Children whose needs are not identified in time often face a combination of challenges, such as financial vulnerability, overcrowded housing and guardians outside the labour market. Sometimes a child or family member also has a disability, ill health or limited ability to benefit from public support.

When society's support comes too late or not at all, the risks of poorer health, weaker school results and diminished confidence in the future increase. This affects both the child and society as a whole.

In this exploratory seminar, we discuss preventive and early interventions. What do our youngest children need, and what must we understand, change and do differently to reach the children we fail to see in time and reverse today's trend?

content.title: Investment plan for Sweden — how can we secure forthcoming major investments in welfare?
content.description: The coming years require extensive investment in municipalities and regions, including upgrading large parts of the country's water and sewer networks and adapting society to climate change.
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities and regions invest more than SEK 230 billion annually. These investments are crucial to ensuring equitable welfare nationwide, as well as strengthening Sweden's long-term growth and competitiveness. SKR has developed a consolidated investment plan for municipalities and regions up to 2040 — Investeringsplan för Sverige.

The coming years will require extensive reinvestment, including upgrades to the country's water and sewer networks, much of which were expanded in the 1960s and 1970s. At the same time, investment needs are growing to adapt buildings, roads and other infrastructure to a changing climate.

Investment needs exist nationwide, but conditions vary and risk hitting some municipalities and regions particularly hard. The seminar explores these needs, the available financial conditions and what is required of municipalities, regions

content.title: What do we do with children who murder?
content.description: The rise of serious crime involving children in Sweden is alarming. Criminal networks are recruiting ever younger children to commit serious violent offences, murder and drug trafficking. What are the alternatives to imprisoning children, and how do we reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
How did we get here? What can and should society do when prevention has failed and we face the fact that a thirteen-year-old has shot another person dead? And is prison really the best measure to stop this development and change the children's course?

Join a seminar discussing societal developments, children involved in crime, what we can and should do to reach them before it is too late, and what we can and should do when the worst has already happened.

In response to the debate, Akademikerförbundet SSR has produced a memorandum highlighting an alternative to prison: nationally specialised treatment services.

content.title: Figures guiding forestry: what must future forest owners know, and where does the information come from?
content.description: Forests must meet many needs: production, recreation, carbon storage, biodiversity and preparedness. What must Swedish forest owners know to develop their forests according to their own plans and society's expectations? How do we know their decision-making information is reliable? Who is responsible for what?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish forests provide many things, including industrial raw materials, a foundation for local economies, carbon storage and climate regulation, culture, tradition and biodiversity. Their role has broadened in recent years, and developments affect more actors nationally and internationally. Policies in an increasing number of areas target forests directly or indirectly.

How should Swedish forest owners navigate an increasingly complex world? What expectations and requirements face today's and tomorrow's owners? Where should they obtain new knowledge and reliable decision support? What must forest owners know, and where is that knowledge available? Who is responsible for ensuring it exists: landowners, market actors or the state?
content.subject: Climate/environment
speakerTitles: Professor of Forest Genetics and Plant Physiology

content.title: Threats and violence against social services
content.description: What happens to social services when managers, social workers and municipal politicians face direct violence? What is needed to protect public representatives from risking their lives and health while carrying out their duties, while also safeguarding open and legally sound decision-making?
content.extendedDescription:
Threats and violence against social services representatives are a structural problem affecting both legal certainty and the working environment. But are systematic, long-term organisational measures enough to bring about real change towards a zero-violence vision? What are we not doing today that we should be doing?

Threats and violence also affect individuals directly and often force personal decisions in which victims must choose between their role and job and their life, health and family. Anonymous decisions are one proposal frequently raised in the debate. How can we balance transparency in decision-making with protecting decision-makers?

Discussion leader and moderator: Lina Blombergsson, Deputy Chair, Föreningen Sverige socialchefer.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Investing before the flood: how private capital creates public value
content.description: Climate change is driving increasing natural disaster damage and major societal costs. Sweden's water and wastewater infrastructure needs hundreds of billions in investment to prevent risks. Yet opportunities to use private capital for climate adaptation are limited.
content.extendedDescription: Cloudbursts, floods and billions in natural disaster damage: climate change is already here, and the bill is growing rapidly. Water and wastewater networks are an area with major investment needs and are important to Sweden's climate adaptation. Almost SEK 600 billion is needed by 2040, but current regulations limit financing through private capital. Occupational pension providers' primary task when managing capital is to generate secure returns for future pensions. A distinctive feature of occupational pension capital is its suitability for long-term investments such as infrastructure projects. What role can private capital and the insurance industry play in reducing climate-related natural disaster risks for society and individuals?
content.detail: Folkhälsodalen, in the garden behind S:t Hans café.

content.title: Growth in transition: who sets Sweden's direction?
content.description: What roles should central government and regional actors play in improving investment and business conditions? How do we balance growth against other important values? How do we establish lasting rules that strengthen competitiveness and hold up during transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces major choices. The need for economic growth is clear, while demands for sustainability, faster processes and clearer priorities between societal interests are increasing.

County administrative boards play a central role, particularly through permitting responsibilities and representing the state regionally. Meanwhile, companies seek better conditions, greater predictability and shorter lead times. How do these perspectives meet, and where do tensions arise?

What roles should the state and regional actors play in improving investment and business conditions? How do we balance growth against other values? How do we create lasting rules that strengthen competitiveness and withstand transition?

Business and political perspectives meet to discuss what is needed to accelerate growth throughout the country.

content.title: Is public transport ready for self-driving vehicles, and what role should it play in their development?
content.description: Autonomous transport is entering real traffic. The question is not whether it is coming, but who shapes it. Shared travel will be crucial to public benefit. Integration into public transport is key. What initiatives do public transport actors need to take to steer development?
content.extendedDescription:
Public transport faces major challenges today: rising costs, difficulty providing adequate access in smaller towns, driver shortages and increased competition from cars and new mobility services, while demands for accessibility, climate benefits and efficient resource use keep growing.

The question is whether autonomous vehicles will worsen these problems or become part of the solution. As the technology moves from pilots to commercial operation, regions and public transport authorities face a crucial choice. Should they wait, or actively steer development towards shared, resource-efficient mobility services that strengthen public transport?

This session focuses on that choice. How can autonomous mobility services be integrated into public transport? What does the sector need to move from testing technology to changing the system?
And what role must public transport actors play to steer development in the right direction?

content.title: Democratic Security Cooperation in a World of Competing Crises: Sweden and the Indo-Pacific
content.description: Sweden has a long history of cooperation and engagement in the Indo-Pacific. Developments in the Indo-Pacific are becoming more important for long-term security, trade, and international partnerships. How can we sustain cooperation across regions?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar ambassadors from Japan, Australia and New Zealand and a leading Swedish academic will discuss democratic security cooperation between Sweden and Indo-Pacific democracies in a global context characterised by a range of crises.
 
An important topic is how like-minded democracies can maintain cooperation despite geographic distance and differing regional priorities. They will also discuss how economic coercion, maritime security challenges, and strategic competition shape relations within the Indo-Pacific, as well as between the Indo-Pacific and Europe.
 
Another focus will be on the implications for Sweden’s security policy and its cooperation with Indo-Pacific democracies, including multilateral frameworks and NATO-related activities. The seminar highlights the need to actively maintain focus on long-term partnerships and shared security interests, and to ensure that cooperation between like-minded democracies is not sidelined when crises “in between” dominate attention.

content.description: How can universities deal with the pressure regarding competitiveness, demography and geopolitics?
content.extendedDescription:
In spite of considerable differences, Japan and Sweden offer interesting university sector comparisons and challenges, such as:

1. Although Sweden’s highly educated population is often considered a key to the ability to punch above its weight Japan has a higher share of young people in tertiary education.
2. While Sweden has a smaller population than Japan, the Swedish university sector as a whole is relatively strong.
3. The Japanese population is shrinking rapidly. In Sweden the number of deaths will likely outnumber births in 2026; very soon the number of potential students will decrease substantially.
 
Questions to discuss concern how the two countries’ university models can deal with the challenges:

1. Should the private sector take greater responsibility in funding higher education?
2. How can universities adapt to shrinking populations?
3. Should politicians take greater responsibility in defining research priorities for the universities?

content.title: Energy production and defence – Gotland leads the way
content.description: Many societal interests collide on Gotland. A strong defence is needed for obvious reasons, while energy supplies must function both under normal conditions and during heightened alert. Region Gotland presents its roadmap for how the island can operate in island mode if cut off.
content.extendedDescription:
Gotland has four major national interests.
1. Försvarsmakten has re-established its presence and is expected to double its operations. 2. Heidelberg Materials in Slite will soon be the country's only cement production site. 3. Heidelberg must become fossil-free through a CCS facility, as its products form part of many industries' value chains. 4. The ferry services, procured by the state, must also become fossil-free.

All four interests are energy-intensive.

Meanwhile, Försvarsmakten is now blocking almost all new local energy production, even though total defence requires substantial local electricity and fuel supplies to remain operational over time.

Region Gotland presents its roadmap for reconciling energy production and defence. Länsstyrelsen presents the FRAMAT project, which works on coexistence. National and international energy experts comment. Political representatives reflect on how the next government needs to act to resolve this.

content.title: Electrifying heavy transport – why do solutions get stuck in the electricity grid?
content.description: Sweden must meet ambitious climate targets, but the electrification of heavy transport essential to society is progressing too slowly. A crucial obstacle is the behaviour of electricity grid companies: monopoly operators that control the conditions without taking responsibility for the results.
content.extendedDescription:
With lengthy processing times and enormous connection charges, electricity grid companies put obstacles in the way of transport companies seeking to lead the transition. Verdis has the will, capacity and ability to electrify waste collection in Stockholm and other municipalities right now. Yet it faces a system that holds it back rather than enables it. Why is doing the right thing so difficult? This seminar identifies who is responsible for advancing the issue and creating the right conditions, and who needs to do more.

What requirements can politicians set to make public procurement an effective tool for the transition? How can municipal politicians steer municipal companies so that they, too, contribute to climate and environmental targets? Electrifying heavy transport requires political will, smart procurement and grid owners who take their share of responsibility. Who will lead, and who will be forced to follow? The seminar begins with a networking lunch.

content.title: Can we innovate as if lives were at stake when they are not? Lessons from Ukraine's drone war
content.description: Can we innovate as if lives were at stake when they are not? Driven by necessity, Ukraine has developed inexpensive drones to disable expensive weapons systems. The pace of innovation is exceptionally high. New drone models, for example, can be invented and developed in just a few weeks.
content.extendedDescription:
The military works seamlessly with public authorities, NGOs and startups towards the same goal. Sweden supports Ukraine with money, knowledge and equipment. What can we learn from their experience? How do we create structures for exchanging innovation that work in both everyday life and crisis? How can cooperation in technological innovation become a natural part of our resilience?

Meet representatives from Ukraine whose different perspectives are important to success at the front. Join a powerful discussion about how drone technology and civil society's capacity for innovation enable Ukraine's successes, followed by a dialogue on how Sweden can prepare for war.

For security reasons, the participants from Ukraine will only be named at the discussion.

content.title: Back to the future – biogas as energy for preparedness
content.description: Untapped biogas production potential could provide energy for preparedness with multiple synergies: greater energy security, reduced dependence on fossil fuel imports, secure gas supplies for industry, transport and electricity generation, and greater food security while reducing climate impact.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish biogas could be key to our energy preparedness. Small and large biogas plants can provide dispatchable, flexible backup power and island-mode operation for municipalities, and local Swedish energy for industry, agriculture and essential services. Residual streams can also become biofertiliser, improving food security. International demand is growing for robust energy systems based on renewable, local resources available during crises. Scaling up our own production can enhance Swedish competitiveness as a leader in circular energy supply.
Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking actors in the built environment sector gather here. This open roundtable shares incisive observations in a solution-oriented discussion of circular value creation and energy preparedness. Together, we create sustainable, resilient communities. Welcome!

content.title: Sweden's most important growth: marine technology and defence innovation for total defence and transition
content.description: In Blekinge, cooperation between the region, municipalities, academia, industry and central government has laid the foundations for one of Sweden's most advanced growth environments. Investment in marine technology and defence innovation has strengthened civilian industry and military capability. How can we use that strength to tackle the energy transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Region Blekinge, Karlskrona kommun and Blekinge Tekniska Högskola, together with Business Sweden, the region's business community, major industrial companies such as NKT and Saab, and authorities such as Försvarsmakten and Kustbevakningen, have cooperated in various ways to create innovation environments, meeting places and research opportunities that accelerate development.

The first discussion highlights successful examples and the most important conditions behind what we have achieved so far, focusing on Blekinge and Karlskrona.

In the second discussion, we broaden our perspective to consider the conditions for stronger total defence capabilities, from both energy supply and security perspectives, taking the Baltic Sea as our starting point.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Knowledge and leadership in an uncertain world: how is Sweden's future being shaped?
content.description: In a time of growing uncertainty, it is important to ask how our knowledge can best be used. What is needed to make the right decisions, and how do we ensure universities' expertise and leadership are actually used to shape a stronger, more resilient society?
content.extendedDescription:
Geopolitical instability, AI's rapid advance and growing skills shortages are putting Sweden under pressure. At a pivotal moment for the knowledge society, three of the country's most influential academic leaders meet to discuss power, responsibility and leadership.

The heads of Karolinska Institutet, KTH and Stockholms universitet join Anna Serner to discuss universities' role in social development and how they can strengthen Sweden's innovation, competitiveness and ability to navigate a rapidly changing world.

A conversation for anyone making decisions, investing in the future or leading in uncertain times. Organised by Stockholm Science City in cooperation with Karolinska Institutet, KTH and Stockholms universitet.

In connection with this seminar, Universitetsalliansen Stockholm trio is organising ‘World-class research: what investments and reforms are needed in Sweden and the EU?’ at 13.45–14.45.

content.title: European copyright – how do we protect what we create?
content.description: Visual art, music, literature and journalism are pillars of our society. You encounter copyrighted material every day, so what happens if that protection is weakened?
content.extendedDescription:
This year, the European Commission is evaluating the effects of the new copyright law that came into force in Sweden in 2023. It is based on an EU directive intended, among other things, to strengthen protection for authors and performing artists.

During this discussion, we present the results of a new survey mapping how sectors have responded to implementation – has protection become stronger in practice? We also discuss what we can expect from the evaluation. Does current copyright protection need to be strengthened at European level?

Politics, culture, academia and law meet in an engaging discussion about how we should protect what we create.
content.subject: Culture
speakerTitles: Legal Adviser, IT and Media Law

content.title: Where did renewables go – and how do energy choices affect climate and biodiversity?
content.description: The expansion of renewable electricity generation has slowed, as has electrification. How can we reverse this trend to secure lower emissions, sufficient electricity, competitiveness and consideration for nature? What roles do efficiency, flexibility and eco-labelled electricity play in a robust energy system?
content.extendedDescription:
What happened to renewables, and how can we take the next step in the energy transition? Sweden is falling behind on electrification, transport emissions are increasing and the expansion of renewable electricity generation has slowed. How does this affect Sweden's competitiveness, climate targets and biodiversity?

This Almedalen seminar brings together businesses, politicians, electricity eco-labelling organisations and climate experts to discuss the development of the energy system. How can renewable electricity, energy efficiency and flexibility help meet demand, strengthen security of supply and reduce environmental impact?

The EU Energy Efficiency Directive requires reduced energy use by 2030. How can Sweden achieve the targets, and what effects will this have on society and businesses?

A new report on the environmental benefits of eco-labelled electricity and its significance for climate and biodiversity.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Total defence starts in everyday life – what role does cooperation between social partners play?
content.description: Sweden's security situation affects all central government operations. Total defence is built not only through plans and structures but through daily life in government workplaces. How is robustness created in the central government sector, and how does the Swedish model contribute to the functioning of total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
The current international situation affects conditions for the central government sector. Security, information influence operations and preparedness place new demands on organisations. Against this backdrop, local social partners must be able to engage in informed dialogue and cooperate on operational issues relating to security and preparedness. Karin Lönnheden of Myndigheten för psykologiskt försvar describes today's reality and tomorrow's security requirements. Drawing on the report 'Öppenhet och säkerhet inom statliga myndigheter' (Openness and security in government agencies), produced by Centrum för totalförsvar och samhällets säkerhet at Försvarshögskolan, the discussion continues with local and central social partners.
Questions include:
What does the changed security situation mean for government operations in practice?
How are managers, employees and relations between social partners affected by heightened preparedness?
Why are trust and dialogue crucial to total defence too?
How can local social partners contribute to the state's collective resilience?
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: What should knowledge cost?
content.description: Students spend an average of SEK 730 a month on course literature and study materials. In most cases, this does not cover all the literature on their reading lists, and just over 90 percent of students think course literature is too expensive.
content.extendedDescription: Lower prices are by far the most important issue for students. 60 percent say that lower literature costs would make them less likely to download it illegally. According to students themselves, prices need to fall by between 25 and 50 percent. But is that possible? If not, how do we solve the funding issue?

content.title: Is the Swedish language dying out?
content.description: English-language course literature has become commonplace in higher education, despite research showing we learn less effectively when we do not read in our mother tongue. What are the consequences?
content.extendedDescription:
The dominance of English-language course literature leads students to fall behind in their reading. Studies from Chalmers show that English course literature is increasingly common even in courses taught entirely in Swedish, and in some programmes it is the norm rather than the exception.

What consequences does this have for students' learning and Swedish's status as an academic language? We know people learn better in their first language, so why do we continue to let English take over?

Welcome to a panel discussion on the importance of language for learning, education and academic discourse.

content.title: Is the right to learning materials secured?
content.description: Teachers can now buy learning materials to a greater extent than before, yet inequalities are still not decreasing. What is needed in learning materials going forward, and what can we expect after the election?
content.extendedDescription: It is two years since pupils' right to learning materials was written into the Education Act, and schools have been able to apply for government grants to buy learning materials for the past three years. Yet inequalities between subjects, schools and municipalities are still not decreasing. Why? 1 in 6 schools has shortcomings in pupils' access to learning materials, according to a review by Skolinspektionen covering 30 schools in total. The findings form an interim report on an assignment given to the agency by the government, with the final review to be presented this autumn. What results can we expect? And how should we think about the future of learning materials after the election?

content.title: Essential transport in peace, crisis and war
content.description: Sweden's transport capability is crucial to business, security of supply and total defence. A deteriorating international situation demands robust freight transport, sufficient rail capacity and clear coordination to keep society functioning during disruptions, crises and heightened alert.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar consists of opening perspectives followed by a panel discussion on strengthening Sweden's transport capability amid a deteriorating international situation. Its starting point is that functioning transport is crucial to business deliveries, society's security of supply and total defence's operational capability.

Particular attention is given to rail and freight transport during disruptions, crises and heightened alert. The discussion addresses measures to ensure long-term robustness, capacity, redundancy and coordination, and how responsibilities and priorities should be shared between public and private actors.

The event begins with a welcome, followed by a keynote and commentary, and ends with a panel discussion. It is aimed at decision-makers and actors in transport, business, security of supply and total defence. No preparation is required.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
