content.title: What happens when municipal housing companies sell their homes?
content.description: When municipalities sell municipal housing, the housing market changes fundamentally. This often leads to higher rents, reduced tenant influence and greater insecurity. The municipality also loses its most important tool for influencing the housing market, including rents, housing availability and social sustainability.
content.extendedDescription: Parts of the municipal housing stock in Örebro, Gävle and Eskilstuna have been sold to private property companies in successive rounds. These sales have consistently prompted dissatisfaction and protests among affected tenants and Hyresgästföreningen. Hyresgästföreningen Region Aros-Gävle/ Mitt, with help from Mats Wingborg, has therefore produced the report 'vad händer när allmännyttan säljer sina bostäder?' (What happens when municipal housing companies sell their homes?), published on Bostad2030. It will be presented, followed by a panel discussion asking, for example: What happens to people's everyday lives – what kind of security is lost when municipal housing is sold? What happens to the municipality's responsibility and opportunities – are there situations where selling is actually defensible? And what does this mean for future housing policy – how can we meet housing needs without a strong municipal housing sector? What is needed to reverse the trend? What role should municipal housing play in future? You are welcome to come and share your opinion!
content.subject: Construction
speakerTitles: Chair of the Municipal Executive Board

content.title: Crisis as a driving force
content.description: We face several parallel crises, both for our planet and for those of us who live on it.
content.extendedDescription:
War, economic crisis, a changing climate and biodiversity loss – and, on a smaller scale, crises of a more technical construction nature that may seem small compared with war and the climate crisis, but which we nevertheless need to manage alongside the larger crises. Crises force us to do things in new ways, making crisis a driving force for innovation and development.

In this panel discussion, we discuss how the crises we face are driving timber construction forward, with society as the winner.

content.title: MS is more than relapses – how do we take responsibility for the whole disease journey?
content.description: MS is more than relapses. How do we ensure equitable care throughout the disease journey?
content.extendedDescription: MS is a complex disease affecting far more than acute relapses, but healthcare is not always organised to address the whole disease journey. content.title: Asthma, allergies, eczema – new knowledge of type 2 inflammation changes our understanding of atopic diseases
content.description: Asthma, allergies, eczema and nasal polyps – one diagnosis rarely comes alone. If you have one of these conditions, the likelihood of also having at least one more is up to 70%. How can we break down silos and create more multidisciplinary, holistic care for people living with several atopic diseases?
content.extendedDescription:
Live podcast and panel discussion with Manne Forssberg – light lunch provided!

During this seminar, experts guide us through new knowledge about the connections between these diseases and explain how their impact on life can intensify when several occur together. We highlight patient perspectives, reveal often hidden suffering and discuss how healthcare structures can develop. How are atopic diseases connected, and what role does the underlying type 2 inflammation, driven by an overactive immune system, play?

content.title: The new AI industry – how can Sweden benefit from the power-hungry players?
content.description: Sweden is attracting AI data centres – some of the world's most electricity-intensive investments. Which developments create the most value? How should electricity be used as a strategic resource as AI grows? And which “power-hungry players” will become Sweden's next engines of prosperity?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has a strong starting position in the global AI economy. With an almost entirely fossil-free electricity system, plentiful land and competitive electricity prices, the country is attractive to AI data centres – a rapidly growing, electricity-intensive sector.

At the same time, these developments raise important questions. Data centres require large amounts of electricity and grid capacity, but their contribution to employment and local value is debated. How can we ensure that investments strengthen competitiveness and long-term societal value? And how do we design electricity systems and regulations for both industrial electrification and AI's growing demand?

As industrial policy becomes more assertive globally, Sweden faces choices. Should certain uses of electricity be prioritised – and on what grounds? Do we have the potential to become a leading hub in global AI infrastructure?

The seminar brings together perspectives from industry, the energy sector and politics to discuss electricity's strategic role in the AI era.
content.subject: Energy

Head of Budget & Policy to Elisabeth Svantesson

content.title: Luxury or necessity – how should welfare services be funded?
content.description: Have welfare services become a spending trap? How can the finances add up?
content.extendedDescription:
In the TV programme "Lyxfällan", the solution is often to sell assets and cut spending. But what do you do when those "costs" are staff in welfare services?

"Lyxfällan" presenter Magnus Hedberg moderates a discussion with Vision's union president Veronica Magnusson and a panel of politicians and experts, using a budget board that puts welfare services' core mission at the centre.

Have welfare services become a spending trap we can cut our way out of? Or should citizens be able to expect equivalent services wherever they live? Is it efficiency when needs assessors and elderly care managers are forced to ask assistant nurses to shower more people in less time?

When health and social care needs grow faster than the resources provided, Sweden's municipalities and regions face a financial dead end. Major investment in water and wastewater infrastructure is also needed, and the climate issue is more important than ever.

How should welfare services be funded?

content.title: AI without a data strategy delivers neither welfare nor democracy
content.description: Sweden's welfare needs are growing faster than its resources, and AI is often presented as the answer. Yet many AI investments fail to deliver benefits to society. The question is what is needed and how decisions can be scrutinised when AI is used in the public sector.
content.extendedDescription:
AI initiatives that deliver value rarely do so because of the technology alone. It is about information management: how knowledge is structured, who manages it and how data quality work is actually carried out.

It is also a question of democracy. When AI makes or supports public-sector decisions, transparency depends on whether the underlying information is managed and traceable.
The seminar presents practical experiences from several years of AI assignments in the public sector, including at Adda, DIGG, Socialstyrelsen, EKN and Linköpings kommun.

We show where the common barriers lie and what is needed to overcome them: information management, ingestion, business rules, context and organisational ownership.

The event is a 40-minute seminar with an introductory presentation followed by questions.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: The invisible road network – 75% of Sweden's roads are privately maintained
content.description: Did you know that private individuals across the country fund and maintain its longest road network? These roads are important for essential transport, food production and recreation. How should we address the challenges facing privately maintained roads? And how can we ensure their development potential is not lost?
content.extendedDescription:
1.5 million people start their morning on a privately maintained road. These roads are essential for people to reach work, school and healthcare. They are vital for getting food to the table and timber to industry. A changing climate, requirements for greater load-bearing capacity, declining engagement and eroded grants are among the challenges. How can we ensure that those responsible for privately maintained roads in the future have good conditions for developing and maintaining their roads and, ultimately, contributing to a robust society?

Through this seminar, Riksförbundet Enskilda vägar wants to highlight both the strengths and challenges of a system built on local responsibility, individual commitment and cost-effective solutions. Although privately maintained roads make up the majority of roads in Sweden, they are largely invisible in the national debate. We want to change that.
Join us to learn more about privately maintained roads and what is needed for the system to flourish. What is good for privately maintained roads is good for Sweden.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: Equitable crisis communication – reaching even hard-to-reach foreign-born residents
content.description: Clear, reliable information is crucial in crises. Yet important messages do not always reach everyone. Lack of trust, language barriers and different media habits mean some groups, particularly foreign-born residents, risk missing information about crises and preparedness in an increasingly uncertain world.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar presents this year's findings from a recurring nationwide survey of more than 1,000 foreign-born residents who have lived in Sweden for 0-15 years. It provides a current picture of how different groups access public information, their trust in public institutions and barriers to reaching them. This year's focus is preparedness and crisis communication. How do people absorb information about, for example, crisis preparedness, health risks or societal disruptions? Which channels work and which do not? What is needed to ensure even hard-to-reach groups receive information they can understand, find relevant and act upon?

The presentation is followed by a panel discussion on developing more inclusive, accurately targeted crisis and preparedness communication, so we genuinely reach everyone when it matters most.

Wraps are available from 11.15 for the first 40 guests.

content.title: Swedish nicotine innovation in the world – how do we secure competitiveness when Europe applies the brakes?
content.description: Swedish nicotine innovation contributes to smoke-free societies and a growing industry. Last year, Sweden exported nicotine pouches worth 6 billion, an increase of nearly 300% since 2022. How can we secure continued innovation, investment and jobs in Sweden's nicotine industry?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish nicotine innovation employs over a thousand people in Sweden, with a strong presence in areas including Västra Götaland, and generates billions in Swedish export revenues. This development now faces substantial tax and regulatory proposals from the EU, while France is banning white snus entirely and placing the product in the same category as narcotics. In the longer term, this could mean reduced investment and fewer jobs in Sweden, and weaker conditions for a growing European niche in which Swedish companies currently play a leading role.

In this seminar, representatives of the industry, business and politics will discuss how Sweden can remain a leader in nicotine innovation as the EU moves towards tougher taxation and regulation. What is needed to keep nicotine industry jobs, innovation and investment in Sweden while contributing to Europe's global competitiveness?

content.title: Cheaper or more resilient — how do we build the energy system of the future?
content.description: The electrification of society and industrial expansion require investment in energy infrastructure on an unprecedented scale. At the same time, the energy system must deliver electricity at reasonable and competitive prices. How do we prioritise?
content.extendedDescription:
The electrification of society and industrial expansion require investment in energy infrastructure on an unprecedented scale. At the same time, the energy system must deliver electricity at reasonable and competitive prices. The deteriorating geopolitical situation demands greater preparedness to secure supplies: energy infrastructure must be not only efficient but also robust and resilient to disruption.

Are more power lines the solution — or can we use the energy system more intelligently?
Svenska kraftnät is investing SEK 225 billion in the transmission grid up to 2035. But major challenges remain in regional and local grids, where capacity shortages hinder new industrial development. The gas grid provides flexible energy, for example through gas turbines when demand peaks. This can both ease pressure on the electricity system and strengthen Sweden's security-of-supply preparedness.
So how do we prioritise?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Customers, capital, skills or rules – what kills growth?
content.description: Sweden produces world-class startups. Yet surprisingly few make it all the way from promising idea to global growth company. Too many stall or die in the critical phase between product and profitability, often called the ‘Valley of Death’. What is actually stopping them?
content.extendedDescription:

content.title: A narrow view of obesity medicines: when healthcare says no to productivity
content.description: Swedish healthcare and the Swedish economy face a growing productivity problem. Politicians, authorities and employers call for greater healthcare productivity, but what happens when new treatments can actually contribute to it?
content.extendedDescription:
A new generation of obesity medicines has rapidly changed the possibilities for treating excess weight and associated diseases. Yet authorities reject public subsidies, citing costs to regional budgets, although obesity is estimated to cost society over SEK 50 billion annually through sickness absence, healthcare use and lost production.
The paradox is clear: almost one in ten Swedish households already uses injectable weight-loss medicines and pays privately. Society thus signals that treatment is perceived to create considerable value, while the public system declines to invest.
Does Sweden take too narrow a view of productivity and societal economics in healthcare? What happens when effective treatments are seen as costs rather than investments?
Economists, decision-makers, healthcare representatives and pharmaceutical experts discuss obesity, productivity and future healthcare priorities.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Disability rights in the digital era
content.description: Not everyone is equal in the information society. While people in Sweden are increasingly dependent on the digital world in everyday life, it remains inaccessible to many. What risks and opportunities does AI present?
content.extendedDescription:
Wikimedia Sverige invites you to breakfast and a discussion about digital accessibility.

Sooner or later, everyone experiences a disability. You may not be able to hear, see, move or speak in the same way as others. As more and more of our lives move into the digital arena, most services and apps are not designed for everyone to use on equal terms.

Sooner or later, most people will therefore find it much harder to use the internet, one of humanity's greatest inventions.

Wikimedia Sverige is the Swedish support association for Wikipedia, and we invite you to breakfast with a short panel discussion on AI, disability rights, accessibility and universal design on the internet. We welcome disability rights organisations, public authorities, politicians and technology companies that want to build a better world.

The event is organised through the project ‘Ett Wikispeech för alla’, funded by Allmänna arvsfonden.

content.title: How Stockholm can strengthen its position as one of Europe's leading financial capitals
content.description: Ahead of Brexit, discussion focused on which city would replace London as Europe's leading financial centre: Frankfurt, Paris or Amsterdam. But Stockholm, described by The Economist as Europe's new capital of capital because of the country's deep and strong capital markets, was barely mentioned.
content.extendedDescription: Sweden and Stockholm are increasingly cited as a model for Europe as the region seeks to strengthen its capital markets, sharpen competitiveness and find funding for growing challenges. content.title: When stress makes employees want to leave – how do we create sustainable workplaces?
content.description: Stress in society continues to increase, and stress-related sickness absence remains high. Meanwhile, an uncertain labour market creates anxiety about job loss, affecting people's security, health and working lives.
content.extendedDescription:
Employers have extensive responsibility for the working environment, but the issue is complex. What can employers and employees do to promote workplace health and create more sustainable working lives?

If's latest Nordic health report shows that many people work while ill and a significant proportion have considered changing jobs or industries because of work-related stress. The report provides deeper insights into public health challenges in the Nordic countries and highlights how stress, sickness absence and loneliness affect individuals and organisations alike.

The seminar discusses what these developments mean for working life and how employers and employees can work preventively to reduce stress, strengthen health and create workplaces where people want and are able to stay.

content.title: Can a CEO vibe-code a business management system?
content.description: Agentic coding enables more people to build more, faster. But it does not automatically make solutions secure, maintainable or legal. The cost of code is falling. The cost of responsibility is not.
content.extendedDescription:
We explain how we moved from experimentation to verified resilience – and why the answer to almost every AI question in the public sector starts with sovereignty, information management and control over one's own data.

Digitalist has worked on AI deliveries for Socialstyrelsen, Adda, Linköpings kommun and Digg. In parallel, we have tested the limits internally: our CEO has vibe-coded an application that is actually in production. This forced us to build processes for reviewing AI-generated code, subagents that review other agents, hardened containers with SBOMs, and an evidence trail that stands up to audit.

content.title: From vision to reality: accelerating personalised and preventive diabetes care in Sweden
content.description: Nearly 6 million Swedes have a personal connection to diabetes. Smart technology offers enormous untapped potential, yet a recent review shows that the technology struggles to reach people and access is unequal. At the same time, public understanding of the disease and the opportunities offered by technology is limited.
content.extendedDescription:
Modern healthcare involves self-care and digital support. Smart diabetes technology enables solutions that make an immediate difference for both patients and healthcare providers.

For type 2 diabetes alone, the annual cost to society exceeds SEK 20 billion, with 70–80% of direct healthcare costs attributable to complications that can largely be prevented or delayed.

By scaling up the use of medical technology, we can both improve quality of life and achieve better clinical outcomes. There is considerable scope to reverse the trend if we can implement the technology more widely in primary care for people living with type 2 diabetes.

content.title: Businesses have made the transition — but where are the electric cars?
content.description: Swedish businesses have invested billions in electrification, charging infrastructure and new business models to drive the climate transition. Despite this, progress is slow.
content.extendedDescription:
The reason is not a lack of technology or willingness, but changing political conditions. Reduced incentives, unclear ground rules and capacity-based tariffs that undermine profitability are making demand for electric cars hesitant, reducing returns on investment and postponing new initiatives. All this also creates uncertainty among consumers.
Meanwhile, Sweden has been overtaken by its Nordic neighbours. Not only Norway but also Denmark and Finland have a larger share of electric cars thanks to clear policy instruments.
This is also a question of European competitiveness. Industry is shifting production and investment towards electrification to cut emissions and retain jobs in Europe. But without stable political signals to both businesses and consumers, the transition risks losing even more momentum.
This discussion brings together business and politics to explore why the transition is sluggish — and what is needed to regain momentum.

content.title: Professional disobedience: using courage to think outside the box in transition work
content.description: A construction project navigates thousands of rules from idea to completed building. But when these rules become more important than the goal of a sustainable future, our compliance can paradoxically become our greatest risk. Do we dare to challenge the boundaries between what we are used to and what we know must be done?
content.extendedDescription:
The construction and property industry needs to act as though the situation is urgent. Liljewall and Centrum för management i byggsektorn — cmb — therefore invite you to a discussion of new climate leadership and ‘professional disobedience’: the courage to recognise when a process is going wrong and the ability to navigate gaps between legal provisions and established patterns. It means finding room to combine the best of proven methods with a willingness to try something new.

Join a discussion of leadership that dares to challenge the system in practice to build the future!

The seminar forms part of cmb's cooperation with BRG within the EU-funded project Living lab för ett klimatneutralt byggande. Read more about the project on our website below.

content.title: Two years of licensing requirements for sheltered accommodation
content.description: On 1 April 2024, a reform introduced licensing requirements for sheltered accommodation. Since then, around 40 women's shelters have closed their accommodation. What remains are expensive, profit-making private providers, while fewer and fewer children and women are granted protection.
content.extendedDescription:
Since April 2024, sheltered accommodation has required a licence under the Social Services Act. The legislation's original purpose was to improve quality and exclude unscrupulous providers. In practice, however, the reform has had far-reaching consequences.

Many non-profit women's shelters have been forced to close their accommodation, while private providers have gained a larger role, making profits from men's violence against women and children. At the same time, fewer children are placed in sheltered accommodation with their mothers, now that each child requires an individual placement decision.

What happens to support when quality is defined by bureaucracy rather than experience of the consequences of violence? And where do women and children go when the barriers to protection are raised?

Drawing on women's shelters' experiences, research and current analyses, we discuss the reform's actual consequences.

Has the legislation strengthened protection, or weakened it?

content.title: How do we improve integration? Schools as an engine for social mobility
content.description: Integration is a hot topic in political debate. Many believe it should improve, but how is this achieved in practice? All pupils must have the same chance to meet learning goals. Yet every year, 20% leave compulsory school without eligibility for further study. How do we change this?
content.extendedDescription:
Some schools have cracked the code for enabling pupils facing the toughest circumstances to reach the highest goals.

Drawing on concrete examples from Kunskapsskolan and Internationella engelska skolan, both of which have schools with high proportions of pupils from foreign backgrounds, we discuss what actually works for successful inclusion. We invite decision-makers to discuss how to make more happen and spread good examples.

content.title: How club-based sport builds strong communities
content.description: Sedentary lifestyles cost society large sums, while a colder social climate creates a sense of not belonging and being unable to influence things. This is where club-based sport has an important role to play, contributing not only to greater well-being and physical health but also to increased trust between people.
content.extendedDescription:
Join us as Friskis releases figures from a unique report on how the exercise habits of more than half a million members benefit society. This includes reduced sick leave and healthcare costs, but also social capital, which is often less tangible.

More than 12,000 Friskis members have also chosen to volunteer. This makes Friskis a platform for personal development and community where young people in particular have the opportunity to grow as engaged members of society.

The panel features Carolina Klüft, Operations Director at Generation Pep, former track and field athlete and Olympic medallist; Freja Andersdotter, board member of Svensk Friidrott; and Janna Hellerup, Secretary General of Friskis&Svettis.

The seminar also highlights social sustainability, what businesses stand to gain by supporting initiatives that benefit society, and how this work can be carried out. Listen to a conversation with Björn Stenvad, CEO of Rättighetsbyrån, and Ulrika Erkenborn Rugumayo, Account Manager at Aspia.

A light breakfast will be served.

content.title: The neighbourhood police officer: a forgotten model for strengthening safety in vulnerable areas?
content.description: In several vulnerable areas, crime, parallel power structures and low trust in public institutions challenge the effectiveness of the rule of law. A renewed investment in neighbourhood policing could strengthen the state's local presence and increase safety and trust in everyday life.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces growing challenges involving crime, insecurity and parallel power structures in vulnerable areas. This is not only about law enforcement, but the state's fundamental ability to uphold the rule of law in everyday life. When the law's effectiveness weakens, trust in society's institutions also risks eroding.

Meanwhile, local police presence has weakened over a long period through centralisation, police station closures and reduced continuous presence in communities. Several evaluations show that the goal of bringing police closer to citizens has only partly been achieved.

The seminar starts with the short documentary Polisen Ulf, following integration police officer Ulf Boström and his foot patrol work in a vulnerable area of Göteborg. After the screening, we talk with Ulf about how renewed investment in neighbourhood policing can strengthen safety and trust in vulnerable areas.

content.title: How do we make wise choices when innovation becomes infrastructure?
content.description: New technology is fundamentally changing property management, from reactive to predictive. Electric vehicle charging and drone-based inspections are two examples of moving from firefighting to planning ahead. But how do you invest wisely when technology becomes part of a property's infrastructure?
content.extendedDescription:
New technology is changing what it means to own and manage property. What were once individual optional additions are increasingly part of long-term property infrastructure, creating opportunities for proactive, data-driven management.
We illustrate this through two areas: charging infrastructure's evolution from individual stations into complex systems of hardware, payment services, power management and operations; and how drone inspections of roofs and façades transform maintenance from isolated interventions into a continuous data source for property management.

content.title: Can entrepreneurship address both poverty and sustainability?
content.description: How do we create economic development that reduces poverty, creates jobs and stays within planetary boundaries? How can more people – especially women, who often face less favourable economic conditions – gain the opportunity to start and run businesses?
content.extendedDescription:
Hand in Hand Sweden works globally to support people, particularly women, in starting and developing small businesses. This creates jobs, strengthens local economies and makes communities more resilient. Experience shows that entrepreneurship and access to capital are crucial to fighting poverty and enabling sustainable development.
Yet today's economic systems are often dominated by large companies, powerful institutions and production methods that are not always sustainable in the long term. How can entrepreneurs and smaller businesses drive progress towards a more sustainable economy that also includes groups often living in poverty?
Join a breakfast discussion bringing together entrepreneurs, business representatives and politicians to discuss entrepreneurship's role in a sustainable, inclusive economy. Focusing on developing economies and drawing clear parallels with Sweden, we explore how political decisions, capital and skills can create better conditions for growth.
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Entrepreneur, Founder of Kivra and Other Companies

content.title: How to stop labour-related crime in construction
content.description: The construction sector is central to Sweden's competitiveness and societal development. But today we see unscrupulous operators exploiting weaknesses in the system, circumventing regulations and creating unfair competition. This affects the whole built environment sector.
content.extendedDescription:
Labour-related crime and unscrupulous operators distort competition in construction and civil engineering, undermine conditions and put both quality and safety at risk. At the same time, historically large investments are underway in Sweden.
Welcome to a discussion about what is required of the built environment sector to stop labour-related crime: what effect do limits on subcontracting tiers actually have, what responsibility do politicians and government agencies bear, and how do we ensure that the right operators win – and that legitimate businesses are not driven out?

content.title: Sustainable development of attractive cities – how Sweden can lead the way
content.description: Sweden's cities face climate change, security threats and social challenges. How can cities develop to achieve the goal of making Sweden a leader in the sustainable development of attractive cities? What is required of the state, municipalities and business?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's cities face major challenges. Meeting them requires the state, municipalities and business to cooperate on planning, financing and designing tomorrow's cities. Rådet för levande städer invites you to discuss how quality of life can drive the development of climate-neutral, robust and socially sustainable living environments.

The research funding call “Kommuner utformade för framtiden – klimatneutrala, robusta och socialt hållbara” is currently open as part of the cooperation within Rådet för levande städer. The discussion explores the contributions needed from the state, municipalities and business to advance the transition.

Rådet för levande städer has a government mandate to coordinate public authorities' urban development work. The national goal is for “Sweden's cities, according to their circumstances, to develop into vibrant, safe and robust living environments where people enjoy spending time. Sweden should lead the way in the sustainable development of attractive cities.”

content.title: Young people's engagement is changing – is democracy keeping up?
content.description: Young people's engagement is different from yesterday, and in 2040 it will not look like today's. Yet we still try to engage young people as though it were 1993. How can youth movements, parties, civil society and public bodies respond to young people's future civic engagement?
content.extendedDescription:
Young people's circumstances, living conditions and ways of organising change over time. Yet many democratic systems, funding models and organisations still reflect yesterday's forms of engagement.

What happens to democracy when young people engage in new ways and adults struggle to recognise and harness that engagement? Where is the balance between safeguarding traditional democratic structures and welcoming new forms of participation?

This discussion of future engagement explores how society responds to changing youth engagement and how youth movements, civil society, parties and the public sector create conditions for civic engagement in every era. Topics include:
- What will future engagement look like?
- How can systems and organisations respond to different forms of engagement over time?
- How can youth movements find purpose, a role, structures and long-term conditions as young people's engagement changes?
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Semiconductors and the global race – where does Sweden stand?
content.description: Sweden's future competitiveness in semiconductors depends on our ability to turn research into production. How do we create better coordination, long-term investment and the right skills to strengthen Sweden's position in the international race?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has strong research and cutting-edge expertise in semiconductors, but faces crucial challenges in coordination, financing and industrial scale-up. Meanwhile, other countries are making strategic, long-term investments to strengthen their positions.

How can Sweden move from fragmented governance to coordinated efforts? What role do test environments and skills provision play in bringing innovations all the way to market? And how can Sweden position itself in European and global initiatives?

Sweden's future competitiveness, security and exports are closely linked to our ability to act now. What is needed, and what does our shared roadmap look like?

Moderator: Thomas Frostberg, innovation and business journalist
